keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
There is something about me that made the event happen
I can no longer trust my own body

vignette: The artillery had turned the village earth into churning mud, and the burning thatched roofs sent plumes of acrid smoke across the sky. When Lan was thirty, uniformed men seized her shoulders without warning, dragging her across the packed dirt while the heat of the flames blistered the air. She had come to believe that her paralysis in that moment was her own failing, a permanent stain of humiliation that proved something fundamentally flawed in her character. Her body had betrayed her, freezing when it should have fought, and the event had fractured her recollection into glaring blind spots she could not fill no matter how hard she tried. Yet the parts she did remember possessed a brutal clarity; they played in her mind with a stark, undeniable vividness that ordinary days could never match, while the rest of the experience sat outside herself like a stranger’s diary. Over the subsequent decades of displacement and resettlement in the United States, those interpretations shaped her daily survival. Because she was certain she was inherently defective and could never rely on her own physical responses, Lan constructed rigid barriers to keep the past contained. Her convictions of intrinsic fault and humiliation cast a long shadow over her recollection, making the missing pieces feel like moral absences and the vivid fragments feel like irrefutable evidence of her guilt. She began locking every door and window multiple times each evening, and she filled her waking hours with dense memorization of religious texts to keep her thoughts from wandering. When a sudden draft carried the scent of damp garden soil through her classroom window, or when the campus kerosene heater flared with familiar orange tongues, the old panic returned, and her need for control immediately sharpened. The vivid, fragmented recollections of being handled without consent made ordinary movements feel perilous, so she withdrew from the community, avoiding new friendships and closing herself off from the local congregation that had once welcomed her. Now, at eighty, Lan’s role as a religious educator at a suburban community center keeps her in a courtyard where the earth is deliberately turned for planting. Her husband has long since grown used to her flinching, but her relentless avoidance and mental distraction left her senses raw and unmodulated, so the scent of soil and the sight of flames struck her with undiminished, jarring intensity. When the gardener’s spade throws up the heavy, metallic smell of freshly dug loam, or when a well-meaning elder taps her shoulder to ask a question, her hands automatically drift to the back door latch, turning it over and over until the metal clicks. She has kept her mind perpetually occupied with scripture and administrative duties, a habit that solidified over months of quiet isolation. But this relentless mental busyness and ritualistic checking only widened the gaps in her recall, pushing the trauma further into the realm of the unreal and unassailable. The more she avoided connection to protect herself, the more her shame and self-blame crystallized into fixed beliefs; she was convinced she deserved the isolation, and that conviction made her nerves snap at the slightest unannounced contact or flicker of heat. The cycle tightened with each passing season. Her constant vigilance and emotional withdrawal left her exhausted and convinced of her own inadequacy, which in turn made the fragmented, hyper-real memories feel even more like proof of her guilt. Those haunting recollections then flooded her senses the moment she stepped into the courtyard, transforming the scent of earth and the sight of a lit lighter into immediate threats. She found herself checking the classroom locks repeatedly after every session, a compulsion that reinforced her belief that her body could not be trusted and that her past failures were irreversible. Her PCL-5 score of 75 confirmed what the quiet desperation of her daily routine already suggested. The exhaustion of this endless loop finally brought her to the clinic’s waiting room. She sits there hoping that someone might help her dismantle the locks she no longer needs, terrified that without them, the vivid, alien truth of what happened will swallow her whole.
